problem: The answer 'ease-in is slower at midpoint, so blur is shorter there' is not generally true, and 'midpoint' is not defined. For a common quadratic ease-in (distance ∝ t²), the instantaneous speed at the time midpoint equals the average speed, so the blur there is the same as for the linear tween, not shorter. For other easing curves the mid-time blur can be shorter, equal or slightly longer than the linear value. A student who writes the given answer would be marked wrong by a careful examiner.
fix: State the safe rule: average speed and total duration are the same for both tweens, but in an ease-in the object moves slowly at the start and quickly at the end, so the blur is short in the early frames and longest near the last frames; a linear tween gives the same blur on every frame (blur = average speed × shutter time). At the exact mid-time the ease-in blur may be below, equal to, or just above the linear value depending on the easing curve, so do not claim 'shorter' without fixing the curve.

problem: 'An empty keyframe starts a new object in that layer' is misleading. An empty (blank) keyframe holds nothing on the stage; the student then draws or places the new object in it.
fix: Say: a blank keyframe is empty, so nothing from the previous frame carries over; you place the new object in it. The next keyframe after it stores that object's property values.

problem: The Text lane shows only a shape-tween bar over frames 1 to 12, with no keyframe markers at either end, while the Ball lane shows keyframes. A student may conclude that a shape tween needs no keyframes.
fix: Add keyframe markers at frames 1 and 12 on the Text lane (and label it as text broken apart into shapes), so both lanes show that every tween is bounded by two keyframes.
